--- title: "Session 11 — Model Evaluation" subtitle: "Overfitting · Cross-validation · Residual and distribution plots · Tuning" --- ::: {.callout-note} **This chapter answers one question: is the model's score real, or did you get lucky?** **Assumed knowledge:** Session 5 — the train–test split and leakage. Session 9 — fitting a regression and reading MAE, RMSE and R². **The one idea to take away:** **one split is one opinion.** A number from a single train–test split can move by a lot when you change the random seed, and a decision based on a difference smaller than that movement has not been made — it has been guessed. ::: ## 🎯 Learning outcomes {#sec-s11-outcomes} By the end of this chapter you can: 1. Recognise overfitting and underfitting from training and test scores. 2. Explain the bias–variance trade-off in plain words. 3. Run k-fold cross-validation and report a score with its spread. 4. Choose between holdout, k-fold, stratified k-fold, leave-one-out and bootstrapping. 5. Diagnose a model from its residual plot and its error distribution. 6. Tune hyperparameters with grid search without touching the test set. 7. Explain why tuning on the test set invalidates the result. ## How this chapter is organised {#sec-s11-organisation} | Part | Question it answers | |---|---| | [A — The two failures](#sec-s11-a) | *What are the ways a model goes wrong?* | | [B — Validation strategies](#sec-s11-b) | *How do I get a score I can trust?* | | [C — Evaluating with pictures](#sec-s11-c) | *What does the score not tell me?* | | [D — Tuning](#sec-s11-d) | *How do I improve it without cheating?* | # Part A — The two failures {#sec-s11-a} ## 1. Overfitting and underfitting {#sec-s11-topic-1} **A model can fail in two opposite directions.** | | Underfitting | Overfitting | |---|---|---| | The model is | too simple | too complex | | Training score | **poor** | **excellent** | | Test score | **poor** | **poor** | | It has | missed the pattern | memorised the noise | | Fix by | adding features, using a richer model | simplifying, adding data, regularising | **The diagnosis is the gap.** Poor on both means underfitting. Excellent on training and poor on test means overfitting. ::: {.callout-tip title="🧠 Analogy — three students revising"} - The **underfitting** student skimmed one page. They do badly on the practice papers and badly in the exam. - The **overfitting** student memorised every practice paper word for word. Perfect on practice, lost in the exam when the questions are worded differently. - The **good** student learned the method. Slightly imperfect on practice, and fine in the exam. **Only the exam tells them apart** — which is why the test set must stay sealed. ::: ### Demo 1 — watching a model overfit, in one table ::: {#14790648 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, StandardScaler from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import r2_score import pandas as pd line = pd.read_csv("datasets/noisy_line.csv") # 40 points on a noisy straight line x, y = line["x"].values, line["y"].values Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(x.reshape(-1, 1), y, test_size=.35, random_state=0) print(f"{'model':<14} {'train R²':>9} {'test R²':>11} verdict") print("-" * 52) for degree in [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 16]: # StandardScaler between the two steps keeps high powers numerically stable m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr) tr, te = r2_score(ytr, m.predict(Xtr)), r2_score(yte, m.predict(Xte)) verdict = "OVERFITTING" if tr - te > 0.2 else "reasonable" print(f"degree {degree:<7} {tr:>9.3f} {te:>11.3f} {verdict}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model train R² test R² verdict ---------------------------------------------------- degree 1 0.640 0.767 reasonable degree 2 0.643 0.746 reasonable degree 3 0.647 0.717 reasonable degree 5 0.666 0.796 reasonable degree 8 0.707 -2.975 OVERFITTING degree 12 0.722 -44.941 OVERFITTING degree 16 0.717 -187.128 OVERFITTING ``` ::: ::: **Watch the two columns separate.** Training R² climbs steadily as the model is given more freedom — it can always bend closer to points it has already seen. The test score peaks around degree 5 and then falls off a cliff: **−45 at degree 12, −187 at degree 16.** A negative R² means *worse than always guessing the average*. The degree-16 model fits its training data better than any other model in the table and is, on unseen data, far worse than useless. ### Demo 2 — the same thing as a picture ::: {#cell-fig-s11-overfit .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 300).reshape(-1, 1) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2)) for ax, degree in zip(axes, [1, 3, 14]): m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), LinearRegression()).fit(Xtr, ytr) ax.scatter(Xtr, ytr, s=18, label="training") ax.scatter(Xte, yte, s=18, color="orange", label="test") ax.plot(grid, m.predict(grid), "r-", lw=1.8) ax.set_ylim(y.min()-6, y.max()+6) ax.set_title(f"degree {degree}", fontsize=10) axes[0].legend(fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print("Degree 14 passes almost exactly through the blue training points — and swings") print("wildly between them, which is where the orange test points live.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Degree 1 misses the pattern. Degree 14 passes through every training point and is useless between them.](session-11-data-model-evaluation_files/figure-html/fig-s11-overfit-output-1.png){#fig-s11-overfit width=1309 height=341} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Degree 14 passes almost exactly through the blue training points — and swings wildly between them, which is where the orange test points live. ``` ::: ::: ## 2. Bias and variance {#sec-s11-topic-2} **These are the technical names for the two failures.** | Term | Means | Shows up as | |---|---|---| | **Bias** | error from wrong assumptions — the model is too simple to represent the truth | underfitting | | **Variance** | error from sensitivity to the particular training data | overfitting | **The trade-off:** making a model more flexible reduces bias and increases variance. There is a middle point, and finding it is what the rest of this chapter is for. ### Demo 3 — variance made visible ::: {#cell-fig-s11-variance .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline import pandas as pd samples = pd.read_csv("datasets/repeated_samples.csv") # six draws from the same truth grid = np.linspace(0, 10, 200).reshape(-1, 1) fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.3)) for degree, a in zip([1, 12], ax): for sample_id, g in samples.groupby("sample"): xs, ys = g["x"].values, g["y"].values m = make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(degree), LinearRegression()).fit(xs.reshape(-1,1), ys) a.plot(grid, m.predict(grid), lw=1.2, alpha=.8) a.set_ylim(-10, 30); a.set_title(f"degree {degree}: {'low' if degree==1 else 'high'} variance") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print("Left: six nearly identical lines — low variance, the model is stable.") print("Right: six wildly different curves from the same underlying truth —") print(" high variance. Which one you get depends on which rows you happened to draw.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The same model fitted to six different samples from the same source. The flexible model changes shape wildly; the simple one barely moves.](session-11-data-model-evaluation_files/figure-html/fig-s11-variance-output-1.png){#fig-s11-variance width=1089 height=352} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Left: six nearly identical lines — low variance, the model is stable. Right: six wildly different curves from the same underlying truth — high variance. Which one you get depends on which rows you happened to draw. ``` ::: ::: # Part B — Validation strategies {#sec-s11-b} ## 3. Why one split is not enough {#sec-s11-topic-3} **A single train–test split gives you one number, and that number depends on which rows happened to land in the test set.** ### Demo 4 — the same model, twenty different scores ::: {#eba18c4e .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import r2_score feats = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_features.csv") X = feats[["f1", "f2", "f3"]].values y = feats["target"].values scores = [] for seed in range(20): Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3, random_state=seed) scores.append(r2_score(yte, LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte))) scores = np.array(scores) print(f"lowest R² : {scores.min():.3f}") print(f"highest R² : {scores.max():.3f}") print(f"spread : {scores.max()-scores.min():.3f}") print(f"average : {scores.mean():.3f} (± {scores.std():.3f})") print("\nSame model, same data, same code. Only the random seed changed.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` lowest R² : 0.556 highest R² : 0.795 spread : 0.239 average : 0.695 (± 0.063) Same model, same data, same code. Only the random seed changed. ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Report a range, not a point"} If your model scores 0.71 and a colleague's scores 0.74, and single splits vary by 0.15, **you have not shown that yours is worse.** You have shown two draws from overlapping ranges. **Any comparison of two models must use the same folds and account for the spread.** ::: ## 4. K-fold cross-validation {#sec-s11-topic-4} **Cross-validation splits the data into *k* parts, then trains *k* times — each time holding out a different part for testing.** Every row is used for testing exactly once. ```{mermaid} flowchart TB D["all training data, split into 5 folds"] D --> R1["run 1: test on fold 1, train on 2,3,4,5"] D --> R2["run 2: test on fold 2, train on 1,3,4,5"] D --> R3["run 3: test on fold 3, train on 1,2,4,5"] D --> R4["run 4: test on fold 4, train on 1,2,3,5"] D --> R5["run 5: test on fold 5, train on 1,2,3,4"] R1 --> A["average the 5 scores
and report the spread"] R2 --> A R3 --> A R4 --> A R5 --> A ``` ### Demo 5 — cross-validation, fold by fold ::: {#95f03da4 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0) fold_scores = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=cv, scoring="r2") for i, s in enumerate(fold_scores, 1): print(f" fold {i}: R² = {s:.3f}") print(f"\nreport this: R² = {fold_scores.mean():.3f} ± {fold_scores.std():.3f}") print(f"a single split could have given you anything from {fold_scores.min():.3f} " f"to {fold_scores.max():.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` fold 1: R² = 0.703 fold 2: R² = 0.802 fold 3: R² = 0.729 fold 4: R² = 0.732 fold 5: R² = 0.656 report this: R² = 0.724 ± 0.047 a single split could have given you anything from 0.656 to 0.802 ``` ::: ::: ## 5. Choosing a validation strategy {#sec-s11-topic-5} ::: {#f64dfda8 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(f"{'strategy':<24} {'how it works':<44} {'use when'}") print("-" * 108) rows = [ ("Holdout", "one split, e.g. 80/20", "data is huge; you need a quick answer"), ("K-fold", "k splits, every row tested once", "the default"), ("Stratified k-fold", "k-fold keeping class proportions", "classification, especially imbalanced"), ("Leave-one-out", "k = number of rows", "very small datasets; expensive"), ("Bootstrapping", "sample with replacement, many times", "you want a confidence interval"), ("Time-series split", "always train on the past, test on the future","the rows are ordered in time"), ] for r in rows: print(f"{r[0]:<24} {r[1]:<44} {r[2]}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` strategy how it works use when ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ Holdout one split, e.g. 80/20 data is huge; you need a quick answer K-fold k splits, every row tested once the default Stratified k-fold k-fold keeping class proportions classification, especially imbalanced Leave-one-out k = number of rows very small datasets; expensive Bootstrapping sample with replacement, many times you want a confidence interval Time-series split always train on the past, test on the future the rows are ordered in time ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="⚠️ Never shuffle time-ordered data"} Ordinary k-fold shuffles rows, so a model can be trained on **next month** and tested on **last month**. It will look excellent and be worthless, because in production the future is not available. **For anything with a time order, use `TimeSeriesSplit`.** ::: ### Demo 6 — bootstrapping for a confidence interval ::: {#0e3774c7 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import r2_score rng = np.random.default_rng(54) boot_scores = [] for _ in range(500): idx = rng.integers(0, len(X), len(X)) # sample rows WITH replacement oob = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(X)), idx) # rows not drawn = the test set if len(oob) < 5: continue m = LinearRegression().fit(X[idx], y[idx]) boot_scores.append(r2_score(y[oob], m.predict(X[oob]))) lo, hi = np.percentile(boot_scores, [2.5, 97.5]) print(f"bootstrap estimate of R²: {np.mean(boot_scores):.3f}") print(f"95% confidence interval : {lo:.3f} to {hi:.3f}") print(f"\nBased on {len(boot_scores)} resamples. Quote the interval, not the point.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` bootstrap estimate of R²: 0.705 95% confidence interval : 0.562 to 0.802 Based on 500 resamples. Quote the interval, not the point. ``` ::: ::: # Part C — Evaluating with pictures {#sec-s11-c} ## 6. What a score cannot tell you {#sec-s11-topic-6} **A single number compresses every mistake into one figure, and hides where the mistakes are.** Two models with identical R² can be wrong in completely different ways. ### Demo 7 — the residual plot ::: {#cell-fig-s11-residuals .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split import pandas as pd rc = pd.read_csv("datasets/residual_cases.csv") xs = rc["x"].values cases = { "Healthy": rc["healthy"].values, "Missing a curve": rc["curved"].values, "Growing error": rc["growing_error"].values, } fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.2)) for ax, (name, yy) in zip(axes, cases.items()): m = LinearRegression().fit(xs.reshape(-1,1), yy) pred = m.predict(xs.reshape(-1,1)) ax.scatter(pred, yy - pred, s=9, alpha=.6) ax.axhline(0, color="red", lw=1.5) ax.set_title(f"{name}\nR² = {m.score(xs.reshape(-1,1), yy):.3f}", fontsize=9) ax.set_xlabel("predicted"); ax.set_ylabel("residual") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print("All three have a respectable R². Only the first is a model you should ship.") print(" curve → the relationship is not linear; the model is systematically wrong") print(" at both ends and systematically right in the middle") print(" fan → the model is reliable for small predictions and unreliable for large") print(" ones. A single R² averages those two very different situations.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Predicted versus residual. A healthy model shows a shapeless band around zero.](session-11-data-model-evaluation_files/figure-html/fig-s11-residuals-output-1.png){#fig-s11-residuals width=1309 height=340} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` All three have a respectable R². Only the first is a model you should ship. curve → the relationship is not linear; the model is systematically wrong at both ends and systematically right in the middle fan → the model is reliable for small predictions and unreliable for large ones. A single R² averages those two very different situations. ``` ::: ::: ## 7. The distribution of the errors {#sec-s11-topic-7} **Plotting the errors themselves shows whether the model is biased and how bad the worst cases are.** ### Demo 8 — the error distribution, and what it reveals ::: {#cell-fig-s11-errordist .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split shapes = pd.read_csv("datasets/error_shapes.csv") Xa = shapes[["f1", "f2"]].values good_y = shapes["target_normal"].values skew_y = shapes["target_heavy"].values # heavy tails: rare, very large errors fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.2)) for a, (name, yy) in zip(ax, [("Healthy errors", good_y), ("Heavy-tailed errors", skew_y)]): Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xa, yy, test_size=.3, random_state=0) err = yte - LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte) a.hist(err, bins=40); a.axvline(0, color="red") a.set_title(f"{name}\nmean error {err.mean():+.2f}, worst {np.abs(err).max():.1f}", fontsize=9) a.set_xlabel("error") plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print("Both models have a mean error near zero — they are unbiased on average.") print("The right-hand one still has occasional predictions that are badly wrong.") print("If a single bad prediction is expensive, the average was never the right measure.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: errors centred on zero and symmetric — healthy. Right: a long tail, so a few predictions are badly wrong.](session-11-data-model-evaluation_files/figure-html/fig-s11-errordist-output-1.png){#fig-s11-errordist width=1089 height=340} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Both models have a mean error near zero — they are unbiased on average. The right-hand one still has occasional predictions that are badly wrong. If a single bad prediction is expensive, the average was never the right measure. ``` ::: ::: ### Demo 9 — predicted versus actual ::: {#cell-fig-s11-predvsactual .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xa, good_y, test_size=.3, random_state=0) pred = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte) plt.scatter(yte, pred, s=12, alpha=.6) lims = [min(yte.min(), pred.min()), max(yte.max(), pred.max())] plt.plot(lims, lims, "r--", lw=1.5, label="perfect prediction") plt.xlabel("actual"); plt.ylabel("predicted"); plt.legend() plt.show() print("Points above the line: the model predicted too high. Below: too low.") print("A systematic tilt away from the diagonal means the model is biased at one end.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Predicted against actual. Perfect predictions lie on the diagonal.](session-11-data-model-evaluation_files/figure-html/fig-s11-predvsactual-output-1.png){#fig-s11-predvsactual width=684 height=408} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Points above the line: the model predicted too high. Below: too low. A systematic tilt away from the diagonal means the model is biased at one end. ``` ::: ::: ## 8. Learning curves {#sec-s11-topic-8} **A learning curve shows the score as training data increases. It tells you what to do next.** ### Demo 10 — "get more data" or "get a better model"? ::: {#cell-fig-s11-learning .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor curved = pd.read_csv("datasets/curved_truth.csv") # the truth here is a curve Xb = curved[["f1", "f2"]].values yb = curved["target"].values fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.3)) for a, (name, model) in zip(ax, [("Too simple (linear)", LinearRegression()), ("Flexible (deep tree)", DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0))]): sizes, train_s, val_s = learning_curve(model, Xb, yb, cv=5, train_sizes=np.linspace(.1, 1, 8), scoring="r2") a.plot(sizes, train_s.mean(1), "o-", label="training score") a.plot(sizes, val_s.mean(1), "o-", label="validation score") a.set_title(name, fontsize=10); a.set_xlabel("training rows"); a.set_ylim(-.1, 1.05) a.legend(fontsize=8) plt.tight_layout(); plt.show() print("LEFT — both curves flat and low, sitting on top of each other:") print(" the model is too simple. More data changes nothing. Change the model.") print("RIGHT — a gap between the curves that is still narrowing:") print(" the model is learning. More data would still help.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Left: the curves converge at a poor score — more data will not help. Right: a gap that is still closing — more data will help.](session-11-data-model-evaluation_files/figure-html/fig-s11-learning-output-1.png){#fig-s11-learning width=1198 height=352} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` LEFT — both curves flat and low, sitting on top of each other: the model is too simple. More data changes nothing. Change the model. RIGHT — a gap between the curves that is still narrowing: the model is learning. More data would still help. ``` ::: ::: # Part D — Tuning {#sec-s11-d} ## 9. Hyperparameters {#sec-s11-topic-9} **A hyperparameter is a setting you choose before training** — the depth of a tree, the *k* in k-Nearest Neighbours, the strength of a regularisation penalty. The model learns its coefficients; it does not learn these. | Method | How it searches | Use when | |---|---|---| | **Grid search** | every combination you list | few settings, small ranges | | **Random search** | random combinations, a fixed budget | many settings — usually beats grid for the same cost | | **Bayesian optimisation** | uses past results to choose what to try next | training is expensive | ### Demo 11 — grid search, done correctly ::: {#a8cfbb58 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import r2_score Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=.25, random_state=0) grid = GridSearchCV( DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0), param_grid={"max_depth": [2, 3, 5, 8, 12, None], "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 20]}, cv=5, scoring="r2", ) grid.fit(Xtr, ytr) # note: only the TRAINING data goes in here print(f"combinations tried : {len(grid.cv_results_['params'])}") print(f"best settings : {grid.best_params_}") print(f"best CV score : {grid.best_score_:.3f} (measured on the training folds)") print(f"score on the sealed test set: {r2_score(yte, grid.predict(Xte)):.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` combinations tried : 18 best settings : {'max_depth': 12, 'min_samples_leaf': 1} best CV score : 0.944 (measured on the training folds) score on the sealed test set: 0.945 ``` ::: ::: **The test set was used exactly once, at the very end.** The search compared 18 combinations using cross-validation *inside* the training data. ### Demo 12 — what tuning on the test set does The damage from peeking is **selection bias**: when you try many candidates and keep the one that scored highest, the score you kept is partly a measure of luck. Here the signal is genuinely weak, so the candidates are nearly equivalent and "best" is mostly noise — which is exactly the situation where peeking hurts most. ::: {#621eb4d9 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import r2_score weak = pd.read_csv("datasets/weak_signal.csv") # one real driver, buried in noise Xw = weak[[f"f{i}" for i in range(1, 7)]].values yw = weak["target"].values Xtr, Xtmp, ytr, ytmp = train_test_split(Xw, yw, test_size=.4, random_state=0) Xpeek, Xfresh, ypeek, yfresh = train_test_split(Xtmp, ytmp, test_size=.5, random_state=1) candidates = [(d, leaf) for d in [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12, None] for leaf in [1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40, 80]] def score_on(Xset, yset, depth, leaf): m = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth, min_samples_leaf=leaf, random_state=0) return r2_score(yset, m.fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xset)) peeked = {c: score_on(Xpeek, ypeek, *c) for c in candidates} best = max(peeked, key=peeked.get) print(f"settings tried : {len(candidates)}") print(f"best score while peeking : {peeked[best]:+.3f} (max_depth={best[0]}, min_samples_leaf={best[1]})") print(f"that same model, fresh data: {score_on(Xfresh, yfresh, *best):+.3f}") print(f"\nflattery : {peeked[best] - score_on(Xfresh, yfresh, *best):+.3f}") print(f"average candidate, peek set : {np.mean(list(peeked.values())):+.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` settings tried : 56 best score while peeking : +0.084 (max_depth=2, min_samples_leaf=80) that same model, fresh data: -0.204 flattery : +0.288 average candidate, peek set : -0.189 ``` ::: ::: **The reported figure was positive. The truth was negative.** Nothing about that model was good — it was simply the luckiest of 56 draws against one small set of rows, and the score that made it look best was the part that would not repeat. Note that the *average* candidate scored badly on the peek set too. The problem is not that the models were good and got worse; it is that **taking the maximum over many noisy measurements returns an inflated measurement.** ::: {.callout-important title="🔓 The test set is spent after one use"} Every time you look at the test score and change something because of it, you leak a little information into your choices. Do it twenty times and the test set has quietly become a second training set. **The discipline:** 1. Split off the test set and **do not touch it** 2. Do all tuning with cross-validation on the training data 3. Look at the test set **once**, at the very end, and report what it says 4. If you then change the model, you need a fresh test set ::: ### Demo 13 — the whole evaluation, as one report ::: {#d7c332c9 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, KFold, train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, r2_score Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=.25, random_state=0) cv = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0) for name, model in [("Baseline (mean)", DummyRegressor()), ("Linear regression", LinearRegression()), ("Random forest", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=120, random_state=0))]: folds = cross_val_score(model, Xtr, ytr, cv=cv, scoring="r2") model.fit(Xtr, ytr) pred = model.predict(Xte) print(f"{name:<20} CV R² {folds.mean():>6.3f} ± {folds.std():.3f} " f"test R² {r2_score(yte, pred):>6.3f} test MAE {mean_absolute_error(yte, pred):>5.2f}") print("\nThe forest wins, and the ± tells you the win is larger than the fold-to-fold noise.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Baseline (mean) CV R² -0.010 ± 0.009 test R² -0.000 test MAE 3.02 Linear regression CV R² 0.375 ± 0.053 test R² 0.514 test MAE 2.06 Random forest CV R² 0.972 ± 0.006 test R² 0.969 test MAE 0.47 The forest wins, and the ± tells you the win is larger than the fold-to-fold noise. ``` ::: ::: ### ❓ Check yourself **Q1.** Training R² is 0.99, test R² is 0.41. What is happening? - (a) Underfitting. - (b) **Overfitting.** - (c) The model is good. **Q2.** Both scores are around 0.3. What should you do? - (a) Simplify the model. - (b) **Use a richer model or add better features — it is underfitting.** - (c) Collect more rows. **Q3.** Why report R² as 0.71 ± 0.06 rather than 0.71? - (a) It looks more professional. - (b) **A single split can vary by more than the difference you are trying to detect.** - (c) R² is always uncertain. **Q4.** Your data is monthly sales for five years. Which validation? - (a) K-fold with shuffling. - (b) **TimeSeriesSplit — always train on earlier months, test on later ones.** - (c) Leave-one-out. **Q5.** You tried 30 model settings, kept the one with the best test score, and reported that score. What is wrong? - (a) 30 is too many. - (b) **The test set was used to make a choice, so the reported score is optimistic. It is no longer an unbiased estimate.** - (c) Nothing. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers"} **A1 — (b).** Excellent on seen data, poor on unseen data — Demo 1's right-hand column. **A2 — (b).** Poor on both is the underfitting signature. Demo 10's left panel shows what the learning curve looks like. **A3 — (b).** Demo 4 measured a spread of over 0.15 across seeds on the same model. **A4 — (b).** Shuffling lets the model train on the future. It will look excellent and be worthless. **A5 — (b).** Demo 12 measured exactly this gap. ::: # 🎯 Tasks {#sec-s11-tasks} ::: {.callout-note title="✏️ Practise"} **Task 1 — Find the sweet spot.** In Demo 1, add degrees 3, 4, 6 and 7. **Report which degree has the best test R², and how far the training score has run ahead of it there.** **Task 2 — Measure the spread.** Run Demo 4 with 100 seeds instead of 20. **Report the standard deviation, and state the smallest score difference you would be willing to call a real difference.** **Task 3 — Diagnose.** For each pair, say overfitting, underfitting or healthy: train 0.95 / test 0.93; train 0.99 / test 0.52; train 0.44 / test 0.42; train 0.72 / test 0.70. **Task 4 — Tune honestly.** Grid-search a `RandomForestRegressor` over `max_depth` and `n_estimators` using cross-validation on the training set only, then report the test score once. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solutions"} ::: {#956b6b09 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.metrics import r2_score print("Task 3") for tr, te in [(0.95, 0.93), (0.99, 0.52), (0.44, 0.42), (0.72, 0.70)]: if tr - te > 0.2: v = "OVERFITTING — big gap" elif tr < 0.6: v = "UNDERFITTING — poor on both" else: v = "healthy — good, and the gap is small" print(f" train {tr:.2f} / test {te:.2f} → {v}") # Task 2 — how big must a difference be before it means anything? feats = pd.read_csv("datasets/three_features.csv") X = feats[["f1", "f2", "f3"]].values; y = feats["target"].values s = np.array([r2_score(*(lambda a: (a[3], LinearRegression().fit(a[0], a[2]).predict(a[1])))( train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3, random_state=k))) for k in range(100)]) print(f"\nTask 2 — over 100 seeds: mean {s.mean():.3f}, std {s.std():.3f}, " f"range {s.min():.3f} to {s.max():.3f}") print(f" A gap smaller than about {2*s.std():.2f} is inside the noise — do not") print(" claim one model beat another on less than that.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Task 3 train 0.95 / test 0.93 → healthy — good, and the gap is small train 0.99 / test 0.52 → OVERFITTING — big gap train 0.44 / test 0.42 → UNDERFITTING — poor on both train 0.72 / test 0.70 → healthy — good, and the gap is small Task 2 — over 100 seeds: mean 0.709, std 0.060, range 0.545 to 0.827 A gap smaller than about 0.12 is inside the noise — do not claim one model beat another on less than that. ``` ::: ::: :::: ::: {.callout-tip title="✅ Before you move on"} - [ ] I can diagnose overfitting and underfitting from two numbers - [ ] I report a cross-validated score with its spread, not a single split - [ ] I know not to shuffle time-ordered data - [ ] I draw the residual plot before believing the R² - [ ] I tune with cross-validation and touch the test set once - [ ] **Easiest thing to forget:** every peek at the test set spends a little of it.
